levers.label: Demand management & contractor release
levers.hypothesis: 15-25% of SI-delivered change work is low-value, duplicative or zombie projects, and run-side T&M teams are sized to historic, not current, ticket volumes. Stopping work is the fastest, cheapest lever and the one IT is least likely to volunteer.
levers.mechanism: RR = (change share x portfolio cut + run share x release %) x SI pool (contingent + managed). Shrinks contingent and managed pools for all later levers.
levers.timing_note: Jan start, 3-month ramp; contracts with 30-60 day T&M notice
levers.risks: Business pushback on cancelled projects; capacity shortfall if cuts hit critical ops programmes; vendors front-load notice fees.
levers.overlap: Reduces base for levers 3, 4, 6, 7, 8. Must be ring-fenced: freed internal staff absorb work, so no internal labour saving counted.

levers.label: Consulting & advisory spend control
levers.hypothesis: Advisory spend grows without a single owner. A CFO-signed approval gate above a threshold and use of the GCC for analysis can cut 25-40%.
levers.risks: Strategic programmes may lose expertise; spend migrates to SI change orders (watch for leakage).
levers.overlap: Lever 16 pool excludes the cut amount.

levers.label: Relocate onshore contractor roles to the GCC
levers.hypothesis: Many onshore contractor roles (development, test, data, L2 support) do not need to sit in a hub city. Moving them to the offshore centre at roughly a quarter of the cost, after a productivity allowance, is the largest unit-cost arbitrage on offer.
levers.mechanism: RR = relocated heads x (onshore cost - GCC cost x productivity factor). Relocated heads = remaining onshore contractors x %.
levers.benchmark: Captive benchmarks: 70-80% offshore for mature GCCs; 30-60% of onshore contractor roles movable
levers.timing_note: Mar start, 6-month ramp; offshore hiring speed is the constraint
levers.risks: GCC hiring capacity; knowledge loss; SI resistance (lost onsite margin); time-zone for ops-critical systems.
levers.overlap: Uses GCC capacity also needed by levers 4 and 5. Reduces base for 6-8.

levers.label: Insource SI offshore staff into the GCC
levers.hypothesis: Converting SI offshore staff (~$59K) into GCC employees (~$50K effective) saves only ~15-20% per head. The real benefits are control, IP retention and lower attrition. Do it for strategic platforms, not for cost.
levers.mechanism: RR = converted heads x (SI offshore cost - GCC cost x factor)
levers.risks: Non-solicit clauses; SI relationship damage; GCC management bandwidth.

levers.label: Make the GCC substitutive: US workforce reshaping
levers.hypothesis: Core diagnostic: an offshore centre built on top of the home-region base, not in place of it, never reaches the P&L. Fix by (a) moving backfill of leavers to the offshore centre by default, (b) harvesting budgeted vacancies, (c) spans & layers, (d) targeted relocations.
levers.mechanism: RR = attrition leavers x not-backfilled % x (US cost - backfill % x GCC cost x 1.2) + relocated x (US - GCC x 1.2) + US cost x (spans % + vacancy %)
levers.slider_inputs: Not-backfilled %, GCC backfill %, relocation %, spans & layers %, vacancy %, severance multiple
levers.one_time_note: Severance ~0.6x spans saving; ~50% of salary per relocated role; ~$10K hiring per GCC backfill
levers.timing_note: Attrition-paced: Jan start, 12-month ramp (only ~half the run-rate lands in 2027)
levers.risks: Morale and attrition of key talent; reputational risk in the home hubs; ops-critical knowledge concentration.
levers.overlap: Biggest internal pool but slowest. Pays off mostly in the year after the target year.

levers.label: AI-enabled delivery productivity
levers.hypothesis: GenAI coding/testing/AMS tools give 15-30% productivity on SI work. Without contract terms, vendors keep it as margin. An 'AI productivity dividend' clause in SI renewals converts it into lower run cost.
levers.mechanism: RR = remaining SI + managed pool x gain % x captured % - AI tooling cost
levers.risks: Gains are measured in output, not heads; vendors resist; quality and security of AI-generated code.
levers.overlap: Applied after volume levers, before price levers 7-8.

levers.label: Consolidate long-tail SIs
levers.hypothesis: A large share (about 30%) of SI spend sits outside the preferred panel, with weaker rates and no volume leverage. Moving half of it to the panel at 10-15% better rates also builds leverage for lever 8.
levers.mechanism: RR = remaining SI pool x tail share x % moved x rate advantage
levers.risks: Niche skills lost; concentration risk with the panel; small vendors may be diverse-supplier commitments.

levers.label: SI rate card renegotiation
levers.hypothesis: The instinctive lever, and the weakest. Applied to what is left after levers 1-7, a 5-7% cut on reopened contracts yields $2-4M; vendors recover 20-30% through mix and change orders, and are asking for ~3% COLA.
levers.mechanism: RR = remaining SI pool x coverage x headline cut x (1 - leakage)
levers.risks: Quality and attrition of vendor staff; vendor shifts best people to other clients.
levers.overlap: Last in the labour chain, so it only sees the residual pool.

levers.label: Application rationalisation
levers.hypothesis: An airline with a large application estate typically carries 10-20% duplicate or low-use apps. The first wave can retire a few hundred.
levers.mechanism: RR = apps retired x avg run cost x (1 - labour share). Labour share excluded to avoid double count with 3-6.
levers.risks: Data retention and regulatory duties; hidden integrations; business owners resist.
levers.overlap: Reduces software (50%) and cloud (30%) pools for 10-11.

levers.label: Software licence & SaaS optimisation
levers.hypothesis: Shelfware (10-30% of licences unused), premium-tier suite over-licensing and renewals without competitive tension. Airline ops software (crew, ops, revenue management) is sticky and gets lower savings.
levers.mechanism: RR = pool x shelfware % + suite spend x (1 - shelf) x suite % + other x (1 - shelf) x renewal share x renewal cut
levers.slider_inputs: Shelfware %, suite %, renewal share, renewal cut
levers.timing_note: Feb start, 6-month ramp; tied to renewal dates
levers.risks: Audit exposure with large enterprise vendors; price uplifts at renewal (5-10%) offset part of the saving.

levers.label: Cloud FinOps
levers.hypothesis: 20-30% of cloud spend is typically waste (idle, over-sized, uncommitted). Fast and reliable, but small in absolute terms: tens of millions, not hundreds.
levers.risks: Engineering time; consumption growth (~12%/yr) erodes visible savings.

levers.label: Data centre & hardware
levers.hypothesis: Third-party maintenance (30-50% cheaper than OEM), refresh-cycle extension and colo consolidation. Depreciation savings count only if the CFO includes depreciation in the CIO budget.
levers.mechanism: RR = HW maint x TPM % x 40% + depreciation x life % x toggle + colo x consolidation %
levers.slider_inputs: TPM %, life extension %, colo %, depreciation toggle
levers.risks: Mainframe flight-ops systems are off-limits short term; aging kit failure risk.

levers.label: Network & telecom
levers.hypothesis: Carrier re-bid, MPLS to SD-WAN, mobile line audit. Airport circuits are constrained by airport authorities and industry networks.
levers.risks: Outage risk at stations; long carrier terms.

levers.label: End-user & workplace
levers.hypothesis: Device refresh 3 to 4-5 years, standard catalogue, peripheral and print reduction.
levers.risks: Employee experience; frontline device reliability (airport, maintenance).

levers.label: Airline systems & platforms
levers.hypothesis: Per-passenger distribution fees, industry messaging, navigation and weather data: few alternatives and multi-year terms. Treat as largely locked; small wins from volume tiers and message optimisation.
levers.mechanism: RR = partly addressable platform spend x reduction %
levers.overlap: Shown so the MD sees what is NOT addressable.

levers.label: Commercial hygiene
levers.hypothesis: Invoice audit, rate-card compliance, duplicate payments, payment terms and rebates typically recover 0.5-1.5% of third-party spend.
levers.overlap: Applied to spend left after all other levers.

levers.label: Cost-increase containment
levers.hypothesis: The target is a 2027 outlay below 2026, so cost increases (home-region merit, offshore wages, vendor COLA, software uplifts, cloud growth) must be absorbed first. Every increase avoided counts dollar for dollar.
levers.mechanism: RR = SI spend x COLA x % refused + software x uplift x % avoided + cloud x growth x % contained
levers.slider_inputs: % COLA refused, % uplift avoided, % cloud growth contained
levers.benchmark: Only part of the cost increases is contractually contestable; merit and offshore wages are HR policy and left as headwinds
levers.risks: Vendors trade price holds for term or volume; cloud demand gates can slow delivery.
levers.overlap: Acts on the headwinds, not the base, so it never overlaps levers 1-16.
